plain_english: When I see someone worried, I ask: What does this person want? If they didn't want something outside their control, how could they be worried? That's why a musician feels calm when playing alone. But when he walks on stage, he gets anxious — even if he has a good voice and plays well. He wants to perform well AND get applause. But applause isn't up to him. So where he has skill, he feels confident. Bring him someone who knows nothing about music, and the musician doesn't care what that person thinks. But in areas where he has no knowledge or practice, he gets anxious. What area is that? He doesn't understand what a crowd is or what crowd approval means. He's learned to play the lowest and highest notes perfectly. But what praise from many people is, and what power it has in life — he doesn't know and hasn't thought about it. So he has to shake and turn pale. Is anyone really afraid of things that aren't actually harmful?
original_excerpt: When I see a man anxious, I say, What does this man want? If he did not want something which is not in his power, how could he be anxious? For this reason a lute player when he is singing by himself has no anxiety, but when he enters the theatre, he is anxious, even if he has a good voice and plays well on the lute; for he not only wishes to sing well, but also to obtain applause: but this is not in his power. Accordingly, where he has skill, there he has confidence. Bring any single person who knows nothing of music, and the musician does not care for him. But in the matter where a man knows nothing and has not been practised, there he is anxious. What matter is this? He knows not what a crowd is or what the praise of a crowd is. However, he has learned to strike the lowest chord and the highest; but what the praise of the many is, and what power it has in life, he neither knows nor has he thought about it. Hence he must of necessity tremble and grow pale. Is any man then afraid about things which are not evils?

plain_english: No. Is he afraid of things that are bad but still within his control so they might not happen? Of course not. Here's the thing: whatever is outside your will isn't good or bad. And everything that depends on your will is within your power. No one can take these things from you or give them to you unless you choose it. So where's the room for worry? But we worry about our weak bodies, our little possessions, what Caesar might do. We don't worry about what's internal. Do we worry about forming false beliefs? No, because that's in my power. About acting against our nature? No, not even that. When you see someone turn pale, the doctor looks at their color and says this person's spleen is messed up, that person's liver is bad. Do the same thing. Say: this person's desires are messed up, he's off track, he's in a fever. Nothing else changes your color or makes you shake or makes your teeth chatter, or makes a person
original_excerpt: No. Is he afraid about things which are evils, but still so far within his power that they may not happen? Certainly he is not. If then the things which are independent of the will are neither good nor bad, and all things which do depend on the will are within our power, and no man can either take them from us or give them to us, if we do not choose, where is room left for anxiety? But we are anxious about our poor body, our little property, about the will of Cæsar; but not anxious about things internal. Are we anxious about not forming a false opinion? No, for this is in my power. About not exerting our movements contrary to nature? No, not even about this. When then you see a man pale, as the physician says, judging from the complexion, this man's spleen is disordered, that man's liver; so also say, this man's desire and aversion are disordered, he is not in the right way, he is in a fever. original_excerpt: Sink in his knees and shift from foot to foot. Iliad, xiii., 281.

plain_english: This is why Zeno wasn't nervous when he went to meet King Antigonus. The king had no power over anything Zeno valued. And Zeno didn't care about the things the king controlled. But Antigonus was anxious about meeting Zeno. He wanted to impress Zeno — but that wasn't up to him. Zeno, however, didn't care about impressing the king. No skilled person tries to please someone who lacks that same skill.
original_excerpt: For this reason, when Zeno was going to meet Antigonus, he was not anxious, for Antigonus had no power over any of the things which Zeno admired; and Zeno did not care for those things over which Antigonus had power. But Antigonus was anxious when he was going to meet Zeno, for he wished to please Zeno; but this was a thing external (out of his power). But Zeno did not want to please Antigonus; for no man who is skilled in any art wishes to please one who has no such skill.

plain_english: Should I try to please you? Why? I suppose you know how one person judges another. Have you bothered to learn what makes a person good or bad? And how someone becomes one way or the other? Then why aren't you good yourself? "How am I not good?" he says. Because no good person complains or groans or cries. No good person turns pale and shakes, or asks "How will he receive me? How will he listen to me?" You fool, however it pleases him. Why do you care about what belongs to others? Is it his fault if he receives your words badly? Of course it is. And can one person's fault create evil in another person? No. Then why are you worried about what belongs to others? "Your point is fair. But I'm anxious about how I'll speak to him." Can't you speak to him however you choose? "But I'm afraid I'll get flustered." If you were going to write the name "Dion," would you be afraid of getting flustered? Not at all. Why not? Because you've practiced writing that name, right? Of course. Well, if you were going to read the name out loud, wouldn't you feel confident? And why? Because every skill gives you strength and confidence in the things it covers. Haven't you practiced speaking? What else did you learn in school?
original_excerpt: Should I try to please you? Why? I suppose, you know the measure by which one man is estimated by another. Have you taken pains to learn what is a good man and what is a bad man, and how a man becomes one or the other? Why then are you not good yourself? How, he replies, am I not good? Because no good man laments or groans or weeps, no good man is pale and trembles, or says, How will he receive me, how will he listen to me? Slave, just as it pleases him. Why do you care about what belongs to others? Is it now his fault if he receives badly what proceeds from you? Certainly. And is it possible that a fault should be one man's, and the evil in another? No. Why then are you anxious about that which belongs to others? Your question is reasonable; but I am anxious how I shall speak to him. Cannot you then speak to him as you choose? But I fear that I may be disconcerted? If you are going to write the name of Dion, are you afraid that you would be disconcerted? By no means. Why? is it not because you have practised writing the name? Certainly. Well, if you were going to read the name, would you not feel the same? and why? Because every art has a certain strength and confidence in the things which belong to it. Have you then not practised speaking? and what else did you learn in the school?

plain_english: Logic and clever arguments? What's the point? Wasn't it to speak skillfully? And isn't skillful speaking the same as speaking at the right time, carefully, intelligently, without mistakes, without getting stuck, and with confidence? Yes. So when you're on a horse in an open field, do you worry about fighting someone on foot? Do you worry in something you've practiced when he hasn't? Yes, but that person I'm going to speak to has the power to kill me. Then tell the truth, you miserable man. Don't boast. Don't claim to be a philosopher. Don't refuse to admit who your real teachers are. As long as you give others this handle to grab you by — your body — you'll follow anyone stronger than you. Socrates practiced speaking. He talked that way to tyrants, to judges, even in prison. Diogenes practiced speaking. He talked that way to Alexander, to pirates, to the man who bought him as a slave. These men were confident because they had practiced what mattered. But you? Go back to your own business and stay there. Go sit in a corner and weave your logical puzzles. Offer them to someone else. You don't have what it takes to rule a state.
original_excerpt: Syllogisms and sophistical propositions? For what purpose? was it not for the purpose of discoursing skilfully? and is not discoursing skilfully the same as discoursing seasonably and cautiously and with intelligence, and also without making mistakes and without hindrance, and besides all this with confidence? Yes. When then you are mounted on a horse and go into a plain, are you anxious at being matched against a man who is on foot, and anxious in a matter in which you are practised, and he is not? Yes, but that person (to whom I am going to speak) has power to kill me. Speak the truth, then, unhappy man, and do not brag, nor claim to be a philosopher, nor refuse to acknowledge your masters, but so long as you present this handle in your body, follow every man who is stronger than yourself. Socrates used to practice speaking, he who talked as he did to the tyrants, to the dicasts (judges), he who talked in his prison. Diogenes had practised speaking, he who spoke as he did to Alexander, to the pirates, to the person who bought him. These men were confident in the things which they practised. But do you walk off to your own affairs and never leave them: go and sit in a corner, and weave syllogisms, and propose them to another. There is not in you the man who can rule a state.
